client: I've been really struggling since I started this new job at the marketing agency about six weeks ago. Everyone else on my team seems to know exactly what they're doing, and I'm the only one who came in without any real experience in marketing, so I constantly feel like I'm falling behind or doing things wrong. Honestly, I wasn't sure about coming here today because I don't know if talking about it is actually going to change anything at work.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot of stress and self-doubt right now — and even the way you're speaking reflects how much this has been weighing on you, with a real urgency behind your words. That feeling of being the "only one" who doesn't have it all figured out is incredibly common when stepping into a new role, and it's worth gently questioning whether your teammates' confidence is as complete as it appears from the outside. I'm really glad you came today, because while talking won't directly change your workload, it can help us untangle the thoughts that are making this feel so overwhelming — and that can genuinely shift how you experience and respond to what's happening at work.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying about my teammates maybe not being as confident as they look, but honestly, it's hard to believe that when I watch them in meetings just rattling off ideas and using all this industry language I barely understand. It doesn't feel like an illusion to me — it feels very real that they have something I don't. I guess I'm a little skeptical that just talking through my thoughts is going to make me feel less lost when I'm actually sitting at my desk trying to figure out what I'm doing.
therapist: Your skepticism makes complete sense, and I want to honor that rather than brush past it — there's something real and painful in watching others seem fluent in a language you're still learning. What I'd gently invite you to notice, though, is that six weeks in, you're essentially comparing your internal experience — all the uncertainty and confusion you feel on the *inside* — to your colleagues' external performance, which is a comparison that will almost always feel unfair to you. The goal here isn't to talk you out of reality, but to help you examine whether the story you're telling yourself — that they *have* something you fundamentally *don't* — is the only way to make sense of what you're seeing.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That framing actually makes some sense to me — the inside versus outside comparison thing — but I think where I get stuck is that even if I try to remind myself of that in the moment, the anxiety kind of takes over and I can't think straight. Like last week, my manager asked me a question in front of the whole team and my mind just went completely blank, and afterward I spent the rest of the day convinced everyone now thinks I'm incompetent. It's like knowing something intellectually doesn't stop the feeling from hitting me just as hard.
therapist: The way you're describing that moment — the blank mind, the spiral afterward — and even the speed and tension in your voice right now tells me this isn't just an abstract worry for you, it's something that hits fast and hard in your body before your thinking brain can catch up. What you're describing is really common in anxiety: the feeling hijacks the thought, which is exactly why intellectual reframing alone often isn't enough in the heat of the moment. In CBT, we actually work on building tools specifically for that gap — ways to interrupt the anxiety response *in the moment* — and I'd also want to gently examine that thought "everyone now thinks I'm incompetent," because one blank moment is a very thin thread to hang such a heavy conclusion on.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I do think you're right that it's more of a physical thing than just a thought — like my heart starts racing before I've even processed what's happening. But I guess I'm wondering what these "tools" actually look like, because I've heard things like "just take a deep breath" before and in the moment it feels kind of useless, almost embarrassing to even try. And the part about examining that thought — I hear you, but it genuinely felt like everyone was looking at me differently for the rest of that meeting, so it doesn't feel like a thin thread to me, it feels like evidence.
therapist: The pace and pitch in your voice right now really reflects how alive and present this all still feels for you — this isn't something you've filed away, it's still sitting right there. Your pushback on both points is actually really valuable, because you're right that "just breathe" can feel dismissive, and the tools I'm thinking of are more specific — like learning to notice the *first* physical signal your body sends before the spiral takes hold, so you have a slightly wider window to work with. And on the "evidence" piece, I want to take that seriously rather than dismiss it — what I'd want to explore with you is whether people looking at you in a moment of silence is evidence that they think you're incompetent, or whether that might be one of several explanations for what you saw.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Okay, I can see what you're doing with the alternative explanations thing, and logically I know people could have just been looking at me because that's what you do when someone's speaking. But in that moment, and even now thinking back on it, my gut just insists that it was more than that — like there's this voice in my head that says I'm rationalizing if I try to let myself off the hook. And the early warning signal idea is interesting to me, but I'm honestly not sure I'm self-aware enough in those moments to catch anything before it's already too late.
therapist: There's something really important in what you just named — that inner voice that calls it "rationalizing" when you try to be kind to yourself — and even though your words carry some openness, the softness and speed in your voice suggests you might be holding this quite carefully, like you're not quite sure it's safe to let yourself off the hook. That critical voice isn't protecting you from self-deception; it's actually a really common cognitive pattern where self-compassion gets reframed as weakness or denial, and that's something we can work on directly. And on the self-awareness piece — you actually just demonstrated it right now, noticing your gut response, tracking how the feeling persists even in recall — that *is* the skill, and it's more developed in you than you're giving yourself credit for.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That reframe about self-compassion being mistaken for weakness actually landed a bit — I hadn't thought about it that way, that the voice criticizing me for letting myself off the hook might itself be the problem rather than some kind of honest check. But I'm still not fully convinced I have more self-awareness than I think, because noticing something after the fact in a therapy session feels very different from catching it in real time when my manager is staring at me waiting for an answer. I guess what I'm wondering is whether any of this actually translates to those high-pressure moments, or if it just stays as something I can reflect on later when the stakes are low.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — quick, high, a little pressured — actually mirrors exactly what you're describing, that gap between knowing something and being able to use it when the heat is on, and I want you to know that tension is real and worth taking seriously. The honest answer is that yes, these skills do need to be practiced in lower-stakes moments first, not because the high-pressure situations don't matter, but because that's literally how the brain builds new pathways — you can't install a fire escape during the fire. What I'd want us to do together is deliberately create smaller versions of that pressure here, so that catching the early signal starts to become more automatic before your manager is in the room waiting.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: The fire escape analogy actually makes sense to me, and I like the idea of practicing in smaller moments, but I'm not totally sure what that looks like in practice — like, are we going to roleplay me being put on the spot or something? That feels a little uncomfortable to think about, honestly, because even simulating it in here feels like it could bring up that same embarrassment. I guess I'm willing to try, but I'm also a bit worried I'll just freeze up and feel stupid even in a safe setting, which almost seems worse somehow.
therapist: The softness in your voice alongside those words tells me this takes real courage to even consider — there's a quiet vulnerability in what you just shared that I don't want to rush past. That fear of freezing and feeling stupid *in here* is actually incredibly useful information, because it means the work is already starting — your nervous system is responding to the idea of exposure the same way it does to the real thing, which means we're already close to the material that matters. And I want to reassure you that if you freeze in here, that's not failure — that's actually the exact moment we'd slow down and work with together, rather than something to be ashamed of.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I appreciate you saying that freezing wouldn't be treated as failure, and part of me does believe you mean that — but there's still this worry that even if you don't judge me for it, I'll judge myself, and that might actually make it harder to recover in the moment. It's kind of like knowing the safety net is there but still being terrified of falling. I think I'm willing to try it, but I want to be honest that I'm going into it already bracing for the embarrassment rather than feeling genuinely okay about it.
therapist: The way you're speaking — fast, high, with that edge of tension — tells me this is costing you something just to say out loud, and I want to acknowledge how honest and brave it is to walk toward something while naming clearly that you're already bracing for it. What you just described — "I'll judge myself" — is actually the most important thing we've uncovered today, because that self-judgment is the real source of the sting, not the freezing itself, and that's something we can work on directly and gently. So let's not pretend you're okay when you're not — let's start exactly there, with that bracing feeling, and use it as our first real piece of material to work with together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It's a little strange to hear that the self-judgment is the real issue, because I think I always assumed that was just... me, like a fixed part of how I'm wired rather than something that could actually change. I'm not sure I even know what it would feel like to go through one of those moments at work without that critical voice waiting on the other side of it. But I guess I'm curious enough to see where you're going with this, even if I'm still not fully convinced it's something I can actually shift.
therapist: There's something really significant in what you just said — and even though your words carry a tentative curiosity, the speed and pitch in your voice suggests this is landing somewhere deeper than you might be letting on, like something quietly important is being touched. That belief that the critical voice is just "you," fixed and permanent, is actually one of the most common and most painful myths that keeps people stuck — because it's not your identity, it's a pattern that was learned, which means it can be unlearned. You don't have to be fully convinced yet — that curiosity you just named is genuinely enough to start with.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think what's getting to me is the idea that it was learned, because that makes me wonder where it came from — like, was I always this hard on myself, or did something make me this way? I don't know if I'm ready to go digging into all of that today, it feels like a bigger can of worms than I came in expecting to open. But I also can't quite shake what you said, so I guess that means something.
therapist: The way you're speaking — soft but quick, with that high pitch — tells me this question is stirring something real even as part of you wants to keep the lid on it, and I want to honor both of those impulses at once. You don't have to open that can of worms today, and I mean that genuinely — knowing that something was learned is enough for now, because it cracks open the possibility of change without requiring you to trace every root right this moment. The fact that you can't quite shake it, as you said, is worth holding onto — that's not discomfort to push away, that's curiosity, and it'll still be there when you're ready.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
